idiom_name: platform counting semaphore: permit counter + waiter queue with atomic acquire/release
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: create one semaphore per bounded resource, initialised with the resource's real concurrency ceiling N. Every operation acquires exactly one permit (or k permits for weighted work) immediately before touching the resource, and releases it on every exit path - success, error, timeout, cancellation - using the language's guaranteed-release construct (finally, defer, RAII permit object, withPermit). Decide the admission policy explicitly: block, block with a deadline, try-and-reject, or degrade. Where the language ships the primitive, use it; where it does not, build the counter + waiter queue from a mutex and condition variable, remembering that the hand-rolled form must also handle spurious wakeups and over-release detection (or use a bounded variant).
code_sketch:
slots = semaphore(8)                 # ceiling of the bounded resource

def handle(request):
    slots.acquire()                  # blocks, or try_acquire(deadline) to shed load
    try:
        serve(request)               # at most 8 operations are inside
    finally:
        slots.release()              # on every exit path, including errors

# weighted variant: slots.acquire(k) for an operation needing k units
pitfalls: Releasing on the success path only, so every failure permanently loses capacity until the service starves.
Acquiring without a deadline or cancellation path, which turns a slow holder into an unbounded queue of blocked callers.
Releasing more often than acquiring: the counter is not ownership-checked, so over-release silently raises the ceiling instead of failing. Use a bounded form where available.
Sizing the permit count from a guess instead of the resource's measured capacity, so the bound is either useless or needlessly restrictive.
Mixing an asyncio.Semaphore with threading primitives (or vice versa), causing the event loop to block and deadlocking coroutines.
Releasing a permit from a different thread or context without ownership tracking, which can raise the counter unexpectedly when the releasing context was itself waiting on the same semaphore.

Wrong move: using a one-permit semaphore as a mutex -> it has no owner, so a crashed or exit-taken holder leaves the count decremented with nothing to detect it (Raymond Chen's 'semaphores don't have owners' critique) -> instead: use a real mutex/critical section where ownership and abandonment detection matter, and reserve semaphores for genuinely N-deep resource pools.

Wrong move: assuming the ceiling is enforced because an initial count was passed -> SemaphoreSlim(initialCount) without a maxCount lets CurrentCount silently exceed the initial value on any duplicated release -> instead: construct with an explicit maximumCount so over-release throws SemaphoreFullException instead of widening the limit.

Wrong move: issuing large acquire_many calls against one fair semaphore -> a queued request for k permits blocks every later single-permit caller even when permits are free (documented tokio/Java fair-semaphore behavior) -> instead: give heavy and light work separate semaphores, or use try_acquire with backoff for the large acquisitions.
